questions.title: Three terms
questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: Protecting data and systems from unauthorised access, loss and damage
The right of individuals to control who sees and uses their personal data
Data is accurate, complete and unchanged except by valid updates

questions.title: Security vs integrity
questions.text: State **two** differences between the terms data security and data integrity.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data integrity deals with the validity of data, while security deals with protection of data (1). Data security avoids unauthorised access of data, while integrity avoids human error when data is entered (1). Accept other suitable answers.
scheme.model_answer:
1 Integrity is about the data being valid and correct, while security is about protecting it.
2 Security prevents unauthorised access, while integrity prevents errors when data is entered.

questions.title: Privacy vs security
questions.text: Explain the difference between data privacy and data security.

scheme.mark_scheme: Privacy: who is allowed to see / use personal data, keeping it confidential (1); security: the methods / measures used to protect data from unauthorised access, loss or damage (1)
scheme.model_answer: Privacy is about who is allowed to see and use someone's personal data; security is the set of measures, such as passwords and encryption, that protect the data.

questions.text: The CIA triad stands for [[1]], [[2]] and [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) confidentiality (2) integrity (3) availability

questions.title: Protecting integrity
questions.text: Select the **three** measures that mainly protect data **integrity**.

scheme.mark_scheme: A, B, D

questions.title: Validation and verification
questions.text: Explain how each method helps to keep data integrity, giving an example.

scheme.mark_scheme: Validation: the computer checks data is reasonable / follows rules, e.g. range or format check (1). Verification: checks data was entered / copied correctly, e.g. double entry / visual check (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Validation: the program rejects unreasonable data, e.g. a grade outside 7–12.
Verification: the data is checked against the original, e.g. typing the e-mail twice.

questions.title: Types of measure
questions.text: Match each measure to its type.

left.text: Locked server room with ID cards
Staff training and a privacy policy

questions.title: Why protect data
questions.text: Provide **four** different arguments for the necessity of protecting data and computer systems.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four different (1 each): legal duty / fines under data protection law; privacy of individuals / identity theft / fraud; financial loss / ransom / recovery costs; reputation / trust; business continuity; safety of people; protecting intellectual property
scheme.model_answer:
1 The law requires personal data to be protected; breaking it leads to fines.
2 Leaked data can be used for identity theft.
3 Attacks cause financial loss and recovery costs.
4 Customers lose trust in the organisation.

questions.title: Data protection law
questions.text: Under data protection law, organisations may keep personal data for as long as they want and use it for any purpose.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Data must be used only for its stated purpose and kept no longer than necessary.

questions.title: Hospital
questions.text: Explain why a hospital must protect the privacy, integrity and availability of its patient records.

scheme.mark_scheme: Privacy: health data is personal / confidential; leaks break the law / harm patients (1); Integrity: changed or wrong records could lead to wrong treatment (1); Availability: doctors must access records at any time, e.g. emergencies (1)
scheme.model_answer: Privacy: patients' health information is confidential and leaking it breaks the law. Integrity: if a record were changed, a patient could get the wrong medicine. Availability: doctors need the records immediately in an emergency.

questions.title: Ransomware at school
questions.text: Ransomware locks a school's files just before the exams. Which property of the data is mainly affected?

scheme.mark_scheme: C

questions.title: Secure but not private
questions.text: Explain how a company could keep its customers' data **secure** but still break their **privacy**.

scheme.mark_scheme: The data is protected from hackers by security measures (1), but the company itself uses / shares / sells it without consent or for another purpose (1)
scheme.model_answer: The data may be well protected from hackers, but if the company sells it to advertisers without the customers' consent, their privacy is broken.

questions.title: Key terms
questions.text: A school stores pupils' personal details, grades and medical information in a database.

parts.title: Security vs integrity
parts.text: State **two** differences between the terms data security and data integrity.

scheme.mark_scheme: Integrity: validity of data vs security: protection of data (1); security avoids unauthorised access vs integrity avoids human error when data is entered (1)
scheme.model_answer:
1 Integrity is about valid, accurate data; security is about protecting it.
2 Security stops unauthorised access; integrity stops errors when data is entered.

parts.title: Privacy
parts.text: Explain what data privacy means for the pupils' medical information.

scheme.mark_scheme: Only authorised people (e.g. the nurse) may see / use the medical data (1); it must be kept confidential and used only for its purpose / with consent (1)
scheme.model_answer: Only authorised staff such as the school nurse may see the medical information, and it must be kept confidential and used only for the pupils' health care.

parts.title: Integrity measures
parts.text: Describe **two** measures that help to keep the integrity of the pupils' grades.

scheme.mark_scheme: Per measure: named (1) + how it helps (1). Validation (range check 0–100 rejects impossible marks); verification (double entry / visual check against paper); access rights (only teachers can edit); audit log; backups to restore correct data
scheme.model_answer: 1 A range check rejects any grade outside the allowed range, so impossible values are not saved. 2 Access rights let only teachers change grades, so pupils cannot alter them.

questions.title: Threats
questions.text: The school's data could be lost, changed or seen by the wrong people.

parts.title: Classify
parts.text: Tick (✓) the property of the data mainly threatened in each case.

prefill: A pupil sees another pupil's medical record
A teacher types 9 instead of 6 for a grade
The server fails and the database cannot be opened
A hacker publishes pupils' home addresses

scheme.mark_scheme: Privacy; integrity; availability; privacy (1 each)

parts.title: Measures
parts.text: Describe **one** measure that protects privacy and **one** that protects availability.

scheme.mark_scheme: Privacy: access rights / passwords / 2FA / encryption named (1) + explanation (1). Availability: backups / disk mirroring / UPS / anti-DDoS named (1) + explanation (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Privacy: access rights, so each user only sees the records needed for their job.
Availability: disk mirroring, so if one disk fails the copy keeps the database working.

questions.title: Arguments for protection
questions.text: The director of an online shop says that protecting the shop's data is too expensive.

parts.title: Arguments
parts.text: Provide arguments for the necessity of protecting the shop's data and computer systems.

scheme.mark_scheme: Up to 3 arguments, each identified (1) and explained for the shop (1): legal duty — fines for leaking customers' personal data; customers' privacy — card details used for fraud / identity theft; financial loss — ransom, recovery, lost sales while the site is down; reputation — customers stop buying; business continuity — orders and stock lost
scheme.model_answer: The law requires customers' personal data to be protected, so a leak would bring large fines. Stolen card details could be used for fraud, and customers would stop trusting and using the shop. An attack that takes the website down means no orders can be taken, losing money every hour.

parts.title: Cost
parts.text: Explain why protection may be cheaper for the shop in the long run.

scheme.mark_scheme: The cost of one serious incident (fines, ransom, recovery, lost sales, lost customers) is usually much higher (1) than the cost of security measures such as backups, firewalls and training (1)
scheme.model_answer: A single breach can cost far more in fines, recovery and lost customers than paying for backups, a firewall and staff training.

summary: The meaning of data security, data privacy and data integrity and how they differ, the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability), threats to data — accidental and deliberate, internal and external — with the measures that protect each property, data protection law, and arguments for why data and computer systems must be protected in schools, banks, hospitals and businesses.

blocks.content: Three terms are often confused in exam questions: **data security**, **data privacy** and **data integrity**. They are related, but each answers a different question.

The **protection of data and computer systems** from **unauthorised access**, **loss**, **damage** or **misuse** — whether accidental or deliberate. It is about the **methods** used: passwords, access rights, encryption, firewalls, backups, physical locks.

The **right of individuals** to control **who can see and use their personal data**, and the duty of organisations to keep personal data **confidential** and use it only for the purpose it was collected for.

Data is **accurate, complete, consistent and up to date**, and has **not been changed** except by authorised, valid changes. It is protected by **validation**, **verification**, access controls and backups.

rows: Methods that **prevent unauthorised access**, loss and damage
Hacking, malware, theft, fire, hardware failure
Leaks, selling data without consent, shoulder-surfing
**Human error** during entry, corruption, unauthorised changes
Passwords, encryption, firewalls, backups, physical security
Access rights, encryption, privacy policies, data protection laws
A firewall stops an attacker reaching the school server
Only the nurse can read pupils' medical records
A range check stops a mark of 150 being saved

blocks.content:
- **Data integrity** deals with the **validity** of data, while **security** deals with the **protection** of data.
- **Data security** avoids **unauthorised access** to data, while **integrity** avoids **human error** when data is entered.
- **Security** is the means; **privacy** is the aim of keeping personal data confidential — data can be secure but used in a way that breaks privacy (e.g. sold to advertisers).
Information security aims to protect three properties of data, often called the **CIA triad** (confidentiality, integrity, availability).

items.title: Data privacy (confidentiality)
items.content: Data can be **seen only by authorised people**. *A student's medical record must not be readable by other students.* Protected by passwords, access rights, encryption.

items.title: Data integrity
items.content: Data is **accurate, complete and unchanged** except by authorised, valid changes. *A bank balance must not be altered by an error or an attacker.* Protected by validation, verification, access rights, checksums, backups.

items.title: Data availability
items.content: Data and systems are **accessible to authorised users when they need them**. *The online exam system must work during the exam.* Protected by backups, disk mirroring, redundant hardware, protection against DoS attacks.

blocks.title: Threats to each property
rows: Hacker reads personal data; shoulder-surfing a password
Virus corrupts files; operator types the wrong value; unauthorised edit
Hardware failure, power cut, DDoS attack, ransomware
Backups, RAID mirroring, UPS, firewalls, anti-malware

blocks.content: Keep the three apart: **privacy** = who can **see** it; **integrity** = is it **correct**; **availability** = can it be **used when needed**.

blocks.title: Kinds of threat
rows: Typing errors, deleting a file by mistake, spilling coffee on a laptop, losing a USB drive
An employee copying customer data to sell, changing records for personal gain
Fire, flood, power cut, hardware failure, lightning
Hacking, malware, phishing, DDoS attacks, theft of equipment

blocks.title: Types of protection measure
rows: Locked server rooms, ID cards, CCTV, fire alarms, UPS, cable locks
User names and passwords, two-factor authentication, access rights, encryption, firewalls, anti-malware
Validation (range, presence, type, format), verification (double entry, visual check), checksums, parity bits
Regular backups, off-site / cloud copies, disk mirroring (RAID 1)
Privacy policies, staff training, audit logs, least-privilege access, disposal procedures

blocks.title: Validation and verification protect integrity
blocks.content:
- **Validation** — the computer checks that data is **reasonable**: a pupil's grade must be 7–12 (range check), the e-mail must contain "@" (format check).
- **Verification** — checks that data was **entered or copied correctly**: the password is typed **twice** (double entry), the operator **compares** the screen with the original form (visual check).
- A **checksum** is calculated before and after data is transmitted; if the values differ, the data was corrupted.

blocks.title: Data protection law
blocks.content: The **Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan "On personal data and its protection"** (and the EU's **GDPR**) require organisations to collect personal data only **with consent** and for a **clear purpose**, keep it **accurate** and **secure**, store it no **longer than necessary**, and let people **see and correct** their data. Breaking the law can lead to **fines** and legal action.

theory.title: Why data and systems must be protected

items.title: Legal and ethical reasons
items.content:
- **Legal duty:** data protection laws require organisations to keep personal data secure; breaking them leads to **fines** and court cases.
- **Privacy of individuals:** leaked personal data can lead to **identity theft**, **fraud**, **blackmail** or **discrimination**.

items.title: Financial reasons
items.content:
- **Stolen money**, **ransom** payments, the cost of **recovering** systems and data.
- **Lost sales and productivity** while systems are down.

items.title: Organisational reasons
items.content:
- **Reputation and trust:** customers, parents and patients leave an organisation that loses their data.
- **Business continuity:** without data (orders, accounts, medical records) the organisation **cannot work**.
- **Intellectual property:** designs, source code and research must not be stolen by competitors.

items.title: Safety reasons
items.content:
- Attacks on **hospitals**, **transport**, **power** or **water** systems can **endanger lives**.
- Wrong data (integrity) in medical or engineering systems can cause **harm**.

blocks.title: Arguments in context — a school
blocks.content: The school stores students' names, addresses, grades and medical data. If the system is not protected, an attacker could **publish personal data** (privacy), **change grades** (integrity) or **lock the system with ransomware before exams** (availability). The school would break the law and lose the trust of parents.

blocks.title: Arguments in other contexts
rows: Money stolen; balances altered; customers lose trust; heavy fines
Wrong treatment if records are changed; private health data leaked; operations delayed if the system is unavailable
Fraud with card details; orders lost; shop closed during an attack
ID numbers, tax and property records
Identity theft; fake documents; public services stop

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State two differences between the terms data security and data integrity. [2]**
Data **integrity** deals with the **validity / accuracy** of data, while **security** deals with **protecting** data (1). Data security avoids **unauthorised access** to data, while integrity avoids **human error** when data is entered (1).

**Q: Explain the difference between data privacy and data security. [2]**
**Privacy** is about **who is allowed** to see and use **personal data** (1); **security** is the **methods** (passwords, encryption, firewalls) used to protect the data from unauthorised access and loss (1).

**Q: Give two reasons why a hospital must protect its computer systems. [2]**
Patients' **private health data** could be leaked, breaking the law (1); if records were **changed** or **unavailable**, patients could receive the **wrong treatment** (1).

- Using "security" and "privacy" as the same word — **security** is the protection; **privacy** is the right to keep personal data confidential.
- Saying integrity means "data is kept secret" — integrity means data is **correct and unchanged**.
- Giving the same argument twice in different words ("hackers steal data" and "data gets stolen").
- Forgetting **accidental** threats such as human error and hardware failure.
